newsitem.title: FRANCE: Jospin cautiously keeps promises in jaded France.
newsitem.headline: Jospin cautiously keeps promises in jaded France.

text.p: France's new Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin has cautiously started to redeem campaign promises on immigration, jobs and Europe in a jolt for a nation jaded by politicians' unkept pledges.

Buoyed by a honeymoon since taking office last week, Jospin still faces giant problems with a platform including creation of 700,000 youth jobs, no tax hikes and a cut in the working week to 35 hours from 39 over five years with no loss of pay.
"Since it started work, the government is carrying out an exercise new to the French politics of recent years: keeping campaign promises," the left-leaning daily Liberation said in an editorial.

An opinion poll on Wednesday showed 50 percent of voters were confident that Jospin would keep his promises. Thirty eight percent lacked confidence, according to the CSA survey for the weekly Le Nouvel Observateur.
"It's a high level of confidence given the current state of disaffection with politicians in France," said Stephane Rozes, head of political studies at CSA.
"Jospin's image is that of a man without excess, a little colourless, but of one who measures his words and does what he says," he told Reuters.
Rozes said the survey also bolstered Jospin by showing few voters were expecting miracle solutions. Fifty-eight percent of those polled reckoned that change should be spread over time.

Jospin's left-wing government has focused on respecting voters after a campaign accusing conservative President Jacques Chirac and his coalition of failing to keep 1995 pledges of creating jobs and cutting taxes.

Chirac had called the snap parliamentary election wrongly, reckoning voters were still deeply disaffected with the Socialists, who themselves presided over rising joblessness and creeping political sleaze before a right-wing landslide in 1993.

Jospin on Tuesday appointed a mediator to grant residence permits to tens of thousands of illegal immigrants, mostly from Africa, in a step towards keeping a promise to scrap a tough new immigration law.

The government, wanting the European Union to put more stress on jobs, has also requested a delay to study a stability pact limiting the budget deficits of countries that join a single European currency. Jospin has promised no extra austerity to qualify for the euro.

French car maker Renault said on Tuesday it was commissioning an independent study of the planned closure of its Vilvoorde assembly plant in Belgium. Jospin had promised to push Renault to look for alternatives to closing the plant.

Unions, however, said the deal was a fig leaf raising false hopes for the plant's 2,900 workers that would still end in closure. "One can feel it: The new ministers will keep their word but won't go any further," Liberation commented.
The CSA poll, which questioned 1,000 people on Monday, indicated Jospin had broad backing for his EU policy.
Asked about budget limits for qualifying for the euro, 58 percent reckoned the government should re-negotiate the criteria even if it risked jeopardising the shift to the euro.
And just 27 percent preferred the alternative that the government should do everything to respect the criteria, even if it meant austerity. Jospin is to outline his policies in parliament on June 19.
